title: Essentials of Cultivation and Awakening
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Cultivation: to follow the manifesting stream of one's own mind and purify away the habits of delusion.

inline.s: Dream Roaming Collection
Reply to Censor Zheng Kunyan
Ming dynasty
Master Hanshan
, author
Cultivation
: to follow the manifesting stream of one's own mind and purify away the habits of delusion.
Awakening: a single thought suddenly comes to rest, and one sees one's own nature thoroughly.
The manifesting stream of one's own mind: the stream of presently active thoughts.

If we speak of this great matter, although it is inherently complete in every person and fully present in each, lacking not a hair's breadth — what can one do, since from beginningless kalpas the seeds of the root of craving, deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, and the deep dye of habitual defilement have obscured the wondrous luminosity, so that one cannot attain its true benefit? One has always made a living within the delusive shadows of body, mind, and world, and so wanders through birth and death. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appearing in the world with a thousand words and ten thousand phrases and all manner of skillful means, speaking of Chan and speaking of the teachings, do nothing but accord with capacities and circumstances: they are tools for breaking attachment. Originally there is no real dharma to give to anyone.

If we speak of this great matter (the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering of the Buddha's knowledge and vision), although it is inherently complete in everyone and fully present in each, lacking not a hair's breadth, yet unfortunately, since beginningless kalpas the seeds of the habit of craving and desire, deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, and deep habitual defilement have obscured the wondrous luminous true mind, so that its true benefit is not obtained. One has always made a living within the delusive shadow of body, mind, and world, and so wanders through birth and death. The Buddhas and patriarchs appearing in the world with a thousand words and ten thousand phrases and all manner of skillful means, speaking of Chan and speaking of the teachings, do nothing but accord with capacities and circumstances and serve as tools to break living beings' attachment to self and to dharmas. Originally there is no real dharma given to anyone.

The great matter: the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering of the Buddha's knowledge and vision. The Lotus Sutra says: "All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great matter; they wish only to enable living beings to open, to show, to awaken to, and to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision." Opening, showing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision: to open the Buddha's knowledge and vision, to reveal it, to awaken to it, and to enter into it. The root of craving: craving and desire. Craving and desire are the root of affliction, and so they are called the root of craving. Skillful means: the devices, methods, or words adopted in order to guide and teach living beings. Originally there is no real dharma to give to anyone: the Tathagata's teaching is like a finger pointing at the moon (a finger indicating where the moon is), not the bright moon itself (the real dharma). Therefore one must still rely on the finger to see the moon. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "The sutra teachings (the teachings spoken by the Tathagata) are like a finger pointing at the moon; if one then sees the moon, one understands that what is pointed at is after all not the moon. So too are all the Tathagatas' various words and expressions that instruct and reveal to bodhisattvas." Sutra: rendered in Chinese as jing, a conforming scripture; "conforming" means that above it conforms to the wondrous principle of all Buddhas and below it conforms to the capacities of living beings.

As for what is called cultivation, it is simply according with one's own mind and purifying away the shadows of deluded thought and habitual tendency. To apply effort here is what is called cultivation. If a single thought of delusion suddenly comes to rest, and one sees thoroughly that one's own mind is originally perfect, luminous, vast, pure by nature, with not a single thing in it, this is called awakening. It is not that apart from this mind there is something else to cultivate or to awaken to. Since the essence of mind is like a mirror, the shadows of deluded thought and clinging are merely dust on the true mind. Hence it is said: the marks of thought are dust, and the feelings of consciousness are grime. When deluded thoughts melt away, the essence itself appears. It is like polishing a mirror: once the grime is clean, the brightness appears — such is the nature of things.

What is called cultivation is simply according with the manifesting stream of one's own mind and purifying away deluded thought and the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, and delusion. To apply effort here is called cultivation. If one cultivates steadily in this way, and a single thought of delusion suddenly comes to rest, and one sees thoroughly that one's own mind is originally perfect, luminous, vast, pure by nature, with not a single thing in it, this is called awakening. It is not that apart from this mind there is something else to cultivate or to awaken to. For the essence of mind is like a mirror, and the shadows of deluded thought and clinging are dust on the true mind. Hence it is said: the marks of thought are dust, and the feelings of consciousness are grime. When deluded thoughts melt away, the essence itself appears. It is like polishing a bronze mirror: once the dust and grime are wiped clean, the body of the mirror is fully revealed and its brightness appears — such is the nature of things.

Shadows of deluded thought and habitual tendency: deluded thoughts and the habits of greed, anger, and delusion are all illusory and unreal, and so they are called shadows. Dharmata (suchness): that which is natural and does not depend on fabrication.

But our habitual defilement, accumulated over kalpas, is firm and solid, and the root of self-love is deep and hard to pull out. In this life we are fortunate to rely on the intrinsically possessed prajna, whose inner perfuming is the cause, and outwardly to rely on a good teacher's arousing as the condition; thus we know our own original nature, arouse the aspiration, and vow to escape birth and death. To pull out at once the root and stem of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas — is that a small matter? If one is not a person of great strength, who bears it up bare-bodied and goes straight in single-edged, then truly it is difficult beyond difficulty! The ancients said, "It is like one man fighting ten thousand" — these are no empty words.

But the defilement of habit that we have accumulated since beginningless kalpas is firm and solid, and the root of self-love is deep and hard to uproot. In this life we are fortunate to rely on the intrinsically possessed prajna, whose inner perfuming is the cause, and outwardly to rely on a good teacher's arousing as the condition; thus we come to know our own nature, arouse the aspiration, and resolve to escape birth and death. To pull out at once the root of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas — how could this be a small matter? If one is not a person of great strength who bears it up with all one's might and goes straight in single-edged, then to escape birth and death is truly difficult beyond difficulty! The ancients said: to escape birth and death is like one man fighting ten thousand. These are no false words!

Self-love: attachment to the self that one falsely clings to (the five aggregates of body and mind). Intrinsically possessed: that is, the true nature, also called the Buddha-nature. Because the true nature is perfect in ten thousand virtues, not increasing in a sage nor decreasing in an ordinary being — like gold within ore, like a treasure in the dark — it is called intrinsically possessed. Root and stem: the root and trunk of a plant, by which the fundamental part of a thing is meant.

Broadly speaking, in the age of the Dharma's decline there are many cultivators but few who obtain true benefit; many who expend effort but few who gain power. Why is this? It is because they do not find the direct place to begin, and merely take the hearing, seeing, knowing, and understanding of those who came before, along with their words, and use consciousness and feeling to measure and conjecture, suppressing deluded thoughts, doing their work at the gateway of light and shadow. They first store the ancients' profound words and wondrous sayings in their bosoms, take them as real dharma, and make them their own knowledge and views. They never realize that not one bit of this is of any use here; this is precisely what is meant by making understanding depend on another and blocking one's own gate of awakening.

Broadly speaking, in the age of the Dharma's decline there are many cultivators but few who obtain true benefit; many who expend effort but few who gain power. What is the reason? It is because they do not apply effort at the direct place to begin, but only on the hearing, seeing, knowing, understanding, and words of those who came before, using consciousness and feeling to conjecture and suppress deluded thoughts, doing their work at the gateway of light and shadow. They always first store the ancients' profound words and wondrous sayings in their bosoms, take them as real dharma (thinking the finger pointing at the moon to be the moon itself), and take them as their own knowledge and views (this is knowledge and views that are learned, not awakened to, and so they are not one's own knowledge and views). They never realize that these understandings and profound sayings are of no use at all in cultivation and awakening; this is precisely what is meant by making understanding depend on another and blocking one's own gate of awakening.

The gateway of light and shadow: this means that one's seeing of the Way is not genuine. The bright moon in the sky stands for the Way; the moon's reflection in water stands for where the Way flows forth. One should follow the reflection and look up at the moon in the sky, and should not take the moon's reflection in the water to be the true moon.

Master Hanshan said: "One who is not tempered in the midst of objects and conditions is still only concerned with the gateway of light and shadow; when faced with the eight winds of adverse and favorable circumstances, one is shaken and swept away and cannot pass through at all." (Dream Roaming Collection

Miscellaneous Words from Jingshan) The eight winds: the eight winds are the eight favorable and unfavorable circumstances of gain, loss, defamation, eulogy, praise, ridicule, sorrow, and joy. Gain is obtaining advancement; loss is losing and falling back; defamation is being slandered behind one's back; eulogy is being praised behind one's back; praise is being praised to one's face; ridicule is being mocked to one's face; sorrow is the various pains of body and mind; joy is the various pleasures of body and mind. These eight dharmas are always loved or hated by worldly people, and can stir the human heart; hence they are likened to the eight winds.
Now, in doing the work, you must first cut away
(the word here means "to shovel away")

knowing and understanding, and work single-mindedly on a single thought. Truly believe that your own mind is originally utterly clean, not hanging by a single thread, perfectly round and bright, filling the dharma-realm. Originally there is no body, mind, or world, nor any deluded thought or emotional calculation. This very single thought is itself originally unborn. All the various states before you are illusory and unreal; they are only shadows appearing in the true mind.

Now, in doing the work, you must first shovel away knowing and understanding, and work solely and precisely on a single thought. Truly believe that your own mind is originally utterly clean, not hanging by a single thread, perfectly round and bright, filling the dharma-realm. Originally there is no body, mind, or world, nor any deluded thought or emotional calculation. This very single thought is itself originally unborn. All the various states before you are illusory and unreal; they are nothing but shadows appearing in the true mind.

Having seen through them in this way, at the place where deluded thoughts arise and cease, fix your gaze on them. Look: where do they arise from, and where do they cease? Exert yourself and give one thrust
(za)

: no matter what deluded thought it may be, one thrust shatters it, and at once it melts like ice and breaks apart like tiles. You must never follow them in their turning, nor let them continue; this is what Yongjia meant by the need to cut off the mind of continuation.

Having seen through them in this way, at the place where deluded thoughts arise and cease, fix your gaze on them. Look: where do they arise from, and where do they cease? (This is the method of contemplating the mind spoken of below.) Exert yourself and give one thrust, and no matter what kind of deluded thought it is, one thrust shatters it and it vanishes at once. You must never follow it (the deluded thought) in its turning, nor let it continue; this is what Master Yongjia meant by the need to cut off the mind of continuation.
Qu
(qu)

— read as "chyu," meaning to narrow the eyes into a slit and look closely. Press: to squeeze and press out. Yongjia: Chan Master Xuanjue, a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou. After ordination he explored the entire Tripitaka and mastered the Tiantai practice of calm abiding and insight. Later he went to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, was awakened by his words, and departed after a single night, and was then known as "One-Night Awakening." He composed the Song of Realizing the Way, and his Yongjia Collection also circulated widely in the world.
For the false and floating mind has originally no root or trace; you must never take it as a real thing and let it lie across your chest. When it arises, at once shout
(duo, a shout of rebuke)

, and with one shout it vanishes. You must never suppress it, for then you will be led along by it, like a gourd on the water. Just cast body, mind, and world aside, and single-mindedly and precisely raise this one thought. Like a sword sweeping across the sky, whether it be Buddha or Mara, it cuts them all off at once, like cutting through tangled silk. Press and thrust forward with bare strength — this is what is called the straightforward mind and right mindfulness of true suchness. Right mindfulness is no-thought. To be able to contemplate no-thought may be called approaching the Buddha's wisdom.

Because deluded thoughts originally have no root, you must never take them as real things and place them in your chest. When a deluded thought arises, at once shout at it, and with one shout it disappears. You must never suppress thoughts, for then you will turn along with them, like a gourd on the water: press this one down and that one floats up again, without end. Just cast body, mind, and world aside, and single-mindedly and precisely raise this one thought (look at where the deluded thought arises from and where it ceases, or shout as soon as a thought arises). Like a sword sweeping across the sky, whether it be Buddha (a wholesome thought) or Mara (an unwholesome thought), it cuts them all off at once, like cutting through tangled silk. Pressing hard upon the deluded thought with bare strength — this state in which the deluded thought has nowhere to hide is precisely to be mindful of true suchness with a straightforward mind. (Layman Pang said: "Just look at where they arise and cease; this is true suchness.") Right mindfulness is no-thought. To be able to contemplate no-thought may be called approaching the Buddha's wisdom.

Like a gourd on the water: a game that children love to play, pressing gourds down in water. A water jar half a person's height is filled with water and three or five gourds are thrown in. Often as this gourd is pressed down, that gourd floats up; one carefully puts all ten fingers to use, and the situation seems to be under one's control, when a moment's inattention leaves one routed and flustered, yet the fun is endless. Bare strength: also written chi li li, an onomatopoeic word.

As for how to cultivate gradually, Master Hanshan says in the section "The Method of Gradual Cultivation": after sudden awakening, one must cultivate gradually. Yet the work of gradual cultivation has no fixed sequence either. It is simply that in daily life one plants one's feet firmly where no thought has yet arisen, and turns the gaze inward. If a deluded thought arises, immediately investigate this one thought: where does it arise from? When one traces it to the place where the thought arises and finds that it is originally unborn, then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations melt like ice at once. What must be avoided, however, is lacking courageous strength, being unable to seize the throat (the vital point, that is, the place where the thought arises), losing awareness and allowing deluded thoughts to continue — then one sinks into delusion and cannot extricate oneself.

When one first arouses the aspiration to cultivate, one must truly believe in the mind-only Dharma gate. The Buddha said: the three realms are mind-only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only. How much Buddhist teaching merely explains these eight words, so clearly that everyone can come to believe them. Broadly, the two paths of sage and ordinary being are only the two paths of delusion and awakening within one's own mind. All causes and effects of good and evil — apart from this mind, not a single thing can be obtained. For our wondrous nature is natural; it originally does not belong to awakening, so how could it be deluded? In speaking of delusion now, it is only that one does not understand that one's own mind is originally without a single thing, does not realize that body, mind, and world are originally empty, and so is obstructed by them — hence it is called delusion. Because one has always exclusively taken the deluded, arising-and-ceasing mind as real, one takes all the various illusions of the six sense objects and conditions as real.

When one first arouses the aspiration to cultivate, one must truly believe in the mind-only Dharma gate. The Buddha said: the three realms are mind-only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only. How much Buddhist teaching merely explains these eight words, clarifying their meaning so that everyone may believe. Broadly speaking, the two paths of sage and ordinary being are only the two paths of delusion and awakening within one's own mind. All causes and effects of good and evil — apart from this mind, not a single thing can be obtained. Because our wondrous nature is natural; originally it does not belong to awakening, so how could it be deluded? In speaking of delusion now, it is only that one does not understand that one's own mind is originally without a single thing, and has not realized that body, mind, and world are originally empty, and so is obstructed by them — hence it is called delusion. Because one has always exclusively used the deluded, arising-and-ceasing mind to think and calculate, and taken it as real, one takes all the various illusions of the six sense objects and conditions as real.
The three realms are mind-only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only: see the section "Turning Consciousness into Wisdom" in this temple's textbook Essentials of Chan and Pure Land.

Now, arousing the aspiration and turning toward it is the upward step of returning the stream to its source. One must entirely strip away all former knowing and understanding, so that not a bit of knowledge, view, or clever method is of use. Simply see through the body, mind, and world before you at a single glance: they are all floating light and illusory shadows appearing in one's own mind, like reflections in a mirror, like the moon in water. Contemplate all sounds as the wind passing through trees; contemplate all states as clouds floating in the sky — all are changing and unreal things. Not only is it so with what is outside: even the deluded thoughts and emotional calculations of one's own mind, all the seeds of the root of craving, habitual tendencies, and afflictions, are all empty, floating, illusory, and unreal. Contemplate deeply in this way.

Now, arousing the aspiration to escape birth and death is the upward step of returning the stream to the source. One must entirely strip away all former knowing and understanding, so that not a bit of knowledge, view, or clever method is of use. Simply see through the body, mind, and world before you at a single glance: all of it is floating light and illusory shadows appearing in one's own mind, like reflections in a mirror, like the moon in water. Contemplate all sounds as the wind passing through trees; contemplate all states as clouds floating in the sky — all are changing and unreal things. Not only is it so with outer objects: even the deluded thoughts and emotional calculations of one's own mind, all the seeds of the root of craving, habitual tendencies, and afflictions, are all empty, floating, illusory, and unreal. One should contemplate deeply in this way.

Whenever a thought arises, you must resolutely investigate where it comes to rest; never let it pass lightly, and never be deceived by it. Doing the work in this way comes somewhat closer to the genuine. Apart from this, to drag in profound knowledge and views and clever methods to piece things together is entirely irrelevant. Even speaking of doing the work is itself a matter of having no choice. It is like using soldiers: weapons are inauspicious instruments, used only when there is no alternative. The ancients' talk of investigating Chan and raising the huatou was likewise a matter of no choice. Though there are many koans, the huatou of examining truly who is reciting the Buddha's name is the easiest to gain power with amid the dust of afflictions. Though it is easy to gain power with, it is no more than a tile used to knock on the door: in the end it must be thrown away, yet for a time it cannot be dispensed with.

Whenever a thought arises, you must resolutely investigate where it comes to rest, looking at where it arises from and where it ceases. Never let it pass lightly, and never be deceived by it and sink into deluded thought. Doing the work in this way comes somewhat closer to the genuine. Apart from this, to drag in other profound knowledge and views and clever methods to piece things together is entirely irrelevant. Even speaking of doing the work is itself a matter of no choice. It is like using soldiers: weapons are inauspicious instruments, used only when there is no alternative. The ancients' talk of investigating Chan and raising the huatou was likewise something they had no choice but to use. Though there are many koans, the huatou of examining truly who is reciting the Buddha's name is the easiest to gain power with amid afflictions. Though it is easy to gain power with, it is no more than a tile used to knock on the door: in the end it must be thrown away; it is only at the beginning that one cannot do without it for a time.

On the ancients' saying that investigating Chan and raising the huatou is a matter of no choice, Elder Master Xuyun said: "The Chan school chiefly practices investigating Chan, and investigating Chan lies in clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. That is, one must penetrate one's own original face — what is called clearly awakening to one's own mind and thoroughly seeing one's own nature. As for this Dharma gate, from the Buddha's twirling of a flower down to the transmission by Patriarch Bodhidharma to the lands of the East, the methods of beginning the work have changed repeatedly. Before the Tang and Song, the Chan worthies mostly awakened to the Way from a single word or half a phrase. The transmission between master and disciple was nothing but mind sealing mind; there was no real dharma at all. Their daily questions and answers were only the unt tying of bonds as the occasion required, giving medicine according to the illness. After the Song dynasty, people's capacities grew inferior, and they could not practice what was taught. For example, they were told to put everything down, or not to think of good or evil, but they could never put it down and were always thinking either of good or of evil. At this point the patriarchs, having no choice, adopted the method of fighting poison with poison and taught people to investigate koans or look into a huatou. They even insisted on one dead huatou, telling you to bite down tightly and not relax for an instant, like a rat gnawing at a coffin, biting down on one spot and not stopping until it gets through. The purpose was to use one thought to oppose ten thousand thoughts; this is truly a method of last resort. It is like virulent poison in the body: without surgery it is hard to be cured." (The Prerequisites for Investigating Chan) The dust of affliction: the mind toiling over objects of dust; another name for affliction. A tile for knocking on the door: picking up a piece of tile from the ground to knock on the gate of a courtyard; once the gate is open it is thrown away. Tile means a broken piece of tile.

Now, in using this to do the work, you must believe in it thoroughly, rely on it firmly, and bite down hard; you must never waver. You must not be like this today and like that tomorrow, now fearing that you will not awaken, now complaining that it is not profound and wondrous. These calculations and deliberations are all obstacles; they must be pointed out and broken through in advance, so that when the time comes no doubts arise.

Now, in using this huatou (who is reciting the Buddha's name?) to do the work, you must believe in it thoroughly, rely on it firmly, and bite down hard; you must never waver. You must not be like this today and like that tomorrow; now fearing that you will not awaken, now complaining that it is not profound and wondrous. These deliberations and calculations are all obstacles, so they are pointed out and broken through for you in advance, and when the time comes no doubts will arise.

When the work reaches the point of gaining power, outer objects do not enter, and only afflictions within the mind rise up without cause. Perhaps desires surge up, or the mind gives rise to gloom, or all kinds of obstacles appear, until the mind is weary and the strength exhausted, and there is nothing to be done. These are the seeds of habitual tendency from immeasurable kalpas stored in the eighth consciousness; today, pressed hard by the work, they all come forth. Here it is most important to be clear: first you must see through them and pass beyond them; you must never be shrouded by them, never be toyed with by them, never take them as real things. Simply rouse your spirits, summon courage and vigor, and raise your root huatou. Right where these thoughts arise, press on in pursuit: here in me there was originally no such thing — where does it come from? What is it after all? You must resolve to see where it comes to rest. Thrust on in this way, and you will make gods and ghosts weep and vanish without trace. You must drive them all out and kill them all, leaving not a thread. With such effort, you will naturally see good news.

If the work reaches the point of gaining power, outer objects do not enter, and only the afflictions within the mind rise up suddenly for no reason at all. Perhaps desires surge up, or the mind gives rise to gloom, or all kinds of obstacles appear, until the mind is weary and the strength exhausted, and there is nothing to be done. These are the seeds of habitual tendency from immeasurable kalpas contained in the alaya consciousness; today, pressed hard by the work, they all come forth. This is the most critical juncture, and you must know it clearly yourself: first you must see through them and pass beyond them; you must never be shrouded by them, never be toyed with by them, never take them as real things. Simply rouse your spirits, summon courage and vigor, and raise your root huatou (who is reciting the Buddha's name?). If desires and afflictions still circle and will not leave, then right where these thoughts arise, pursue them relentlessly: here in me there was originally no such thing — ask where it comes from? What is it after all? You must resolve to see where it comes to rest. Thrust on in this way, and you will make gods and ghosts weep and vanish without trace. You must drive them all out and kill them all, leaving not a thread. With such effort, you will naturally see good news.
Qu: he, or it.

If a single thought is pressed through, then all deluded thoughts fall away at once, like the shadows of flowers in the sky dropping, like the waves of a mirage becoming clear. Having passed through this once, you gain immeasurable ease and immeasurable freedom. This is where the beginner gains power; it is nothing profound or wondrous. As for ease and freedom, you must not give rise to a mind of delight. If you give rise to delight, the demon of delight attaches to your mind, and you have one more obstacle.

If a single thought is pressed through, then all deluded thoughts fall away at once, like the shadows of flowers in the sky fading, like the waves of a mirage becoming clear. Having passed through this barrier, you gain immeasurable ease and immeasurable freedom. This is where the beginner gains power; it should not be regarded as profound and wondrous. As for ease and freedom, you must not give rise to a mind of delight. If you give rise to delight, the demon of delight attaches to your mind, and you have one more obstacle.

Flowers in the sky: one with diseased eyes sees flowers in space, though space originally has no flowers; it is only the false seeing of the diseased eyes. Flowers in the sky are used to illustrate illusion. The word rendered flower is the ancient form of the modern word for flower. Mirage: a vapor produced under the blazing sun, which from afar looks like water; a thirsty deer longs to drink it but can never obtain it — used to illustrate illusion; one of the ten similes of the Mahayana. Beginner's mind: one who has just aroused the aspiration to study the Buddha's teaching.

As for the seeds of habitual tendency and the root of craving in the storehouse consciousness, they are firm and lie deep. Where the huatou cannot be applied with force, where contemplation of the mind cannot illuminate, where you yourself cannot lay hands on them — you must bow to the Buddhas, recite sutras, and repent, and further you must secretly uphold the mantra-essence, relying on the Buddha's secret seal to dispel them. For all the secret mantras are the Buddha's vajra mind-seal. When we use them, it is like holding the vajra jeweled club, shattering all things; whatever it meets is reduced to dust. The mind-seal secret of all the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old is not beyond this. Hence it is said: "The Tathagatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-essence, attain supreme perfect enlightenment." But whereas the Buddha stated this openly, the patriarchs' gate, fearing that it would fall into ordinary sentiment, kept it secret and did not speak of it — not that they did not use it. This requires a fixed daily practice; after a long time, when it becomes thoroughly familiar, one gains much power from it — but one must not seek miraculous responses.

As for the seeds of habitual tendency and the root of craving in the alaya consciousness, they are firm and lie deep. At such times the huatou is of no use, contemplation of the mind does not reach them, and you yourself cannot lay hands on them. You must then bow to the Buddhas, recite sutras, and repent, and further you must secretly uphold the mantra-essence, relying on the Buddha's secret seal to dispel them. For all the secret mantras are the Buddha's vajra mind-seal. When we recite the mantra-essence, it is like holding the vajra jeweled club in hand: whatever it meets is shattered to dust. The mind-seal secret of all the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times is not beyond this. Hence it is said: "The Tathagatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-essence, attain supreme perfect enlightenment." But whereas the Buddha stated this openly for living beings, the patriarchs' gate, fearing that it would fall into ordinary sentiment, kept it secret and did not speak of it — not that they did not use it. Secret upholding of the mantra-essence requires a fixed daily practice; after a long time, when thoroughly familiar, one gains much power from it, but one must not seek miraculous responses.

Mantra-essence: the most essential part of a mantra. In the Surangama Sutra, after the Buddha had spoken the Surangama Mantra, he called it the mantra-essence. The sutra says: "The Tathagatas of the ten directions, by means of this mantra-essence, attain supreme perfect enlightenment.... The Tathagatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-essence, can bestow a head-anointing and a prediction in the ten directions."

Among cultivators, some awaken first and then cultivate, others cultivate first and then awaken; but awakening differs as understanding and as realization. To clarify the mind according to the Buddha's and patriarchs' teachings is understanding-awakening; it mostly falls into knowledge and views, and is mostly of no use with regard to any object or condition. Because mind and object stand opposed and cannot merge, wherever it touches it becomes stuck and creates many obstacles. This is called semblance prajna, not true investigation. As for realization-awakening, one works plainly from within one's own mind, pressing on to the place where the water runs out and the mountains end, until suddenly a single thought comes to rest and one thoroughly understands one's own mind — like meeting one's own father at a crossroads, with no further doubt. It is like a person drinking water, knowing for oneself whether it is cold or warm, and unable to express it to others. This is true investigation and genuine awakening. Thereafter one uses the place of awakening to merge mind and object, purifying away present karma and the flowing consciousness, so that deluded thoughts and emotional calculations all melt into one flavor of true mind — this is realization-awakening.

Among cultivators, some awaken first and then cultivate (sudden awakening, gradual cultivation), others cultivate first and then awaken (gradual cultivation, sudden awakening); hence awakening differs as understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. To clarify the mind according to the Buddha's and patriarchs' teachings is understanding-awakening. One who understands-awakens mostly falls into knowledge and views, and is mostly of no use with regard to any object or condition. This is because mind and object still stand opposed and have not merged; therefore, when meeting objects and conditions one is entangled and meets many obstacles. This is semblance prajna, not true investigation. As for one who realizes-awakening, he works plainly and steadily from within his own mind (whether by contemplating the mind or by investigating Chan), pressing on to the place where the water runs out and the mountains end, until suddenly a single thought (a subtle thought) comes to rest and he thoroughly awakens to his own mind — like meeting one's own father at a crossroads, recognizing him at a glance without wondering whether it is he. This state is like a person drinking water: only he himself knows whether it is cold or warm, and he cannot tell others of it. Only this is true investigation and genuine awakening. Thereafter he uses the place of awakening to merge mind and object, purifying away present karma and the flowing consciousness, and melting deluded thoughts and emotional calculations all into one flavor of true mind — this is realization-awakening.

This passage says: Chan practice has two paths — sudden awakening with gradual cultivation, and gradual cultivation with sudden awakening — and the meaning of their awakening (seeing the nature) also differs. The awakening of sudden awakening with gradual cultivation is understanding-awakening; the awakening of gradual cultivation with sudden awakening is realization-awakening. The Preface to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan says: "To cultivate because of awakening is understanding-awakening; to awaken because of cultivation is realization-awakening."
This realization-awakening also differs in depth. If one works from the root, breaks through the old rut of the eight consciousnesses
(ke jiu)

, suddenly overturns the den of ignorance, and springs straight through in one leap with no remaining dharma — this is the highest, sharpest capacity, and what is realized is deep. The rest, cultivating gradually, realize shallowly. What is most to be feared is being satisfied with little, and what is most to be avoided is falling into the gateway of light and shadow. Why? Because the root of the eight consciousnesses is not yet broken; even if there is activity, it is all on the side of the spirit of consciousness. If one takes this as real, it is much like taking a thief for one's son. The ancients said: "The student of the Way does not know the true, only because he has always recognized the spirit of consciousness; for immeasurable kalpas it has been the root of birth and death, yet the fool takes it for the original person." This one barrier is what you must above all pass through.

This realization-awakening also differs in depth. If one works from the root (working solely and precisely on a single thought), breaks through the old rut of the eight consciousnesses, suddenly overturns the den of ignorance, and springs straight through in one leap with no remaining dharma — this is a person of the highest, sharpest capacity, and what is realized is deep. The rest, cultivating gradually, realize shallowly. What is most to be feared is being satisfied with little; what is most to be avoided is falling into the gateway of light and shadow and taking it as the ultimate, without going further. Why? Because the root ignorance of the eight consciousnesses is not yet broken; even if there is activity, it is all on the side of the spirit of consciousness (the consciousness-mind). If one takes this as real, it is simply like taking a thief for one's son. The ancients said: "The student of the Way does not know the true, only because he has always recognized the spirit of consciousness; for immeasurable kalpas it has been the root of birth and death (the root of birth and death), yet the fool takes it for the original person." The barrier of falling into the gateway of light and shadow is one you must by all means pass through.

Breaking through the old rut of the eight consciousnesses: breaking through the old pattern in which the eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and alaya consciousness) give rise to mind in dependence on objects — this is the state of great, thorough awakening. Old rut means an established pattern, a worn groove.

Root ignorance: also called beginningless ignorance, namely the true nature, from beginningless time, with a single thought of non-awakening, benighted through the long night, not understanding the truth, able to give rise to all delusions and afflictions.

Taking a thief for one's son: the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says, "Suppose a person takes a thief for his son; the family's wealth will never be secured." Spirit of consciousness: the consciousness-mind. The consciousness-mind is also called the deliberating mind — the mind that arises by clinging to the six sense objects.

What is meant by sudden awakening and gradual cultivation is that one has first awakened thoroughly, but habitual tendencies remain and cannot be purified at once. So in the midst of all objects and conditions, by means of the principle one has awakened to, one brings forth the power of contemplation and examines the mind through each situation. Dissolve one part of the object, and one part of the dharma-body is realized. Eliminate one part of deluded thought, and one part of intrinsic wisdom appears. This depends entirely on fine and continuous work, carried out amid objects and conditions, and it is then all the more powerful.

What is meant by sudden awakening and gradual cultivation is that one has first awakened thoroughly, but habitual tendencies remain and cannot be purified at once. Therefore, in the midst of all objects and conditions, by means of the principle one has awakened to, one brings forth the power of contemplation and examines the mind through each situation. Dissolve one part of the object, and one part of the dharma-body is realized. Eliminate one part of deluded thought, and one part of intrinsic wisdom appears. This again depends entirely on fine and continuous work carried out amid objects and conditions, and it is then all the more powerful.

Intrinsic wisdom: that is, fundamental wisdom, also called non-discriminating wisdom; it is the true wisdom by which Buddhas and bodhisattvas personally realize suchness and accord with the true nature of all dharmas.

Those of sharp capacity and courageous faith who are willing to do the work in cultivation find that the obstruction of things is easily removed, while the obstruction of principle is hard to dispel. Of the ailments here, a few are briefly described below.

Those of sharp capacity and courageous faith are all willing to put in hard work in cultivation; the obstruction of things is easily removed, while the obstruction of principle is hard to dispel. Of the ailments here, a few are briefly described below.

The obstruction of things and the obstruction of principle: afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion can cause birth and death to continue and obstruct great nirvana, and are called the obstruction of things; wrong views can hinder right knowledge and vision and obstruct great bodhi, and are called the obstruction of principle.

1. Do not crave the profound and wondrous. For this matter is originally plain and even, solid and settled, of one plain flavor, with nothing profound or wondrous about it. Therefore the ancients said: "Awakened, one is still the same as before awakening; one is still the same person as before, though not at the same place of practice as before." There is nothing more profound or wondrous. When the work arrives, it is naturally plain and real. It is because our habitual tendencies of knowing and understanding are not yet purified, and inwardly perfume the prajna. When prajna is perfumed by habitual tendencies, it gives rise to illusions and produces many clever views that wrap around the mind, so that one takes them as profound and wondrous and enters deep without letting go. This is precisely the shadowy brightness of the spirit of consciousness, the root of discriminating false views; it is also called a splinter of view. It differs from the earlier coarse, floating deluded thoughts: this is the subtle flowing stream of arising and ceasing, also called the obstruction of wisdom, which precisely obstructs right knowledge and vision. If a person takes it as real, he will give rise to all kinds of wild views. This is what is most to be avoided.

1. Do not crave the profound and wondrous. For this matter is originally plain and even, solid and settled, of one plain flavor, with nothing more profound or wondrous about it. Therefore the ancients said: "Awakened, one is still the same as before awakening; one is still the same person as before (not having added a hair's breadth), though not at the same place of practice as before (after awakening the eye is bright as snow, not deceived by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, so that one deals with objects and conditions differently from before and no longer clings to marks)." Therefore, there is nothing more profound or wondrous. If the work reaches home, it is naturally plain and real. But because our habitual tendencies of knowing and understanding are not yet purified, they inwardly perfume the prajna. When prajna is perfumed by the habitual tendencies of knowing and understanding and measures things with consciousness and feeling, it gives rise to many illusions and produces all kinds of false, profound and wondrous views that wrap around the mind, while one thinks oneself profound and wondrous and enters deep without letting go. How could one know that this is precisely the shadowy brightness of the spirit of consciousness, the root of discriminating false views, also called a splinter of view? It differs from the earlier coarse, floating deluded thoughts: this is the subtle flowing stream of arising and ceasing, also called the obstruction of wisdom, which precisely obstructs right knowledge and vision. If one mistakenly takes it to be a real state, one will give rise to all kinds of wild views. This is what is most taboo in cultivation.

[SECOND, one must not keep the mind in wait for enlightenment. Because our wonderfully perfect, genuine mind is originally without duality. In the past, because of the condensation of delusive thought, mind and objects, faculties and dusts, stand opposed to one another, and therefore one gives rise to delusion and creates karma. Now, for a cultivator there is just a single thought. Let go of body, mind, and the world, and simply hold up this one thought and press forward; do not care whether it is enlightenment or no enlightenment — only keep going, thought after thought, step after step. If the work reaches the point, one will naturally see his original face; why be in a hurry to plan ahead? If one keeps the mind in wait for enlightenment, this very waiting-mind is the root and trunk of birth and death. One may wait until the eons are exhausted and still never awaken, because one has not understood the truly undual mind, and thinks there is something else besides it. If the waiting-mind is not removed, weariness easily arises, and one for the most part falls back. It is like seeking a thing and not finding it, and then giving rise to the thought of stopping and resting.]

Second, do not keep the mind in wait for enlightenment. Because our wonderfully perfect, genuine mind is originally without duality. In the past, because of the condensation of delusive thought, mind and objects, faculties and dusts, stand opposed to one another, and therefore one gives rise to delusion and creates karma. Now, in cultivation one does the work on a single thought. Let go of body, mind, and the world; simply hold up this one thought (mind-contemplation or Chan investigation) and press forward. Do not care whether it is enlightenment or not — only keep doing it, thought after thought, step after step. If the work reaches the point, one will naturally see his original face; why make plans in advance? If one keeps the mind in wait for enlightenment, this very waiting-mind is the root of birth and death. Waiting until the Year of the Donkey and the Month of the Horse, one still cannot awaken. This is because he does not understand the truly undual mind, and thinks there is something else besides it. If the waiting-mind is not removed, weariness easily arises, and one for the most part falls back. It is like seeking a thing and not finding it, and then giving rise to the thought of stopping and resting.

[Without duality (juedai)] To be free of all opposing pairs. Opposing pairs means the mutual opposition of two sides, such as black and white, large and small, good and evil, and so on. Without duality is the equality of thusness, in which no Dharma is obtained, and so it is free of all opposing pairs; for short it is called juedai (without duality). It is synonymous with the absolute.

[THIRD, one must not long for the wonderful fruit. Because the delusive mind of birth and death of sentient beings is originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata. Now, sunk in delusion, [one] transforms the spiritual powers and wonderful functions of the Buddhas into delusive thoughts and feelings and discriminating views; transforms the true and pure Dharma-body into the substance of the karma of birth and death; transforms the pure and wonderful land into the realms of the six dusts. Now, doing the work, if in a single thought one suddenly awakens to his own mind, it is like the great forge, casting and fusing the myriad forms. This very body, mind, and world are originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata; these very delusive thoughts and feelings are originally the spiritual powers and wonderful functions; only the names are changed, not the substance. Yongjia says: “The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the empty body of illusion is the Dharma-body.” If one can awaken to this Dharma-gate, then the feelings of taking and rejecting are forgotten, the mind of delight and disgust is stilled: every step is the Avataṃsaka Pure Land, and every thought is Maitreya's descent into birth [to become a Buddha]. If one first settles the mind seeking the wonderful fruit, this mind of longing is the root of birth and death, and obstructs right knowledge and vision. The more one seeks, the further away one goes; when the strength of seeking is exhausted, weariness arises.]

Third, do not long for the wonderful fruit. Because the delusive mind of birth and death of sentient beings is originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata. (When self-nature is deluded, it is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened, it is a Buddha.) Now, with self-nature sunk in delusion, [one] transforms the spiritual powers and wonderful functions of the Buddhas into delusive thoughts and feelings and discriminating views; transforms the true and pure Dharma-body into the substance of the karma of birth and death; transforms the pure and wonderful land into the realms of the six dusts. Now, in doing the work, if in a single thought one suddenly awakens to his own mind, it is like the great red furnace of that which creates and transforms, casting and fusing the myriad forms. This very body, mind, and world are originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata; these very delusive thoughts and feelings are originally the spiritual powers and wonderful functions; only the names are changed, not the substance. As Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the empty body of illusion is the Dharma-body.” If one can awaken to this Dharma-gate, then the feelings of taking and rejecting are forgotten, the mind of delight and disgust is stilled: every step is the Avataṃsaka Pure Land, and every thought is Maitreya's descent into birth (becoming a Buddha). If one first settles the mind seeking the wonderful fruit, this mind of longing is the root of birth and death, and obstructs right knowledge and vision. The more one seeks the wonderful fruit, the further away one is from realizing the Way; seeking without obtaining, one's strength is exhausted, and weariness arises.
[The great smelter (daye)] A metaphor for that which creates and transforms [creation].

[FOURTH, one must not give rise to doubt oneself. Whenever doing the work, [one should] all along let go of body and mind, and shut off seeing, hearing, perception, and knowing. Having left the old steps behind, looking forward is dim
(in ancient usage the same as “dim and distant”)

and obscure, with no place to settle body and mind. Advancing, there is no new realization; retreating, one loses the old home. If one calculates and worries about front and back, then a doubting mind arises. One gives rise to countless reckonings, weighing gain and loss. Or one engenders arbitrary opinions apart from this, stirring up perverse thoughts, obstructing right knowledge and vision. This must be broken through, and then one proceeds straight in with determination, no longer harboring hesitation. Generally, when the work reaches the point where one can no longer do it, that is precisely where the strength lies; with even greater spirit, one will not retreat or shrink back. Otherwise, one falls into the demon of sorrow.]

Fourth, do not give rise to doubt oneself. Whenever doing the work, once one lets go of body and mind and shuts off seeing, hearing, perception, and knowing, and has left the familiar old road behind, looking forward on the new road it is again strange and boundless, with no place to settle body and mind. Advancing, there is no new realization; retreating, one loses the old home. In such a situation, if one calculates and worries about front and back, then a doubting mind arises. Thereupon one gives rise to countless reckonings, weighing gain and loss. Or one engenders subjective views apart from this, stirring up perverse thoughts, obstructing right knowledge and vision. This point must be broken through, and then one proceeds straight in with determination, no longer harboring hesitation. Generally, when the work reaches the point where one can no longer do it, that is precisely where the strength lies; one should rouse one's spirit further and continue, and then one will not retreat or shrink back. Otherwise, one falls into the demon of sorrow.
[Spirit (jingcai)] Vigor; energy.

[FIFTH, one must not give rise to a mind of terror. This means that when the power of thought in the work is urgent and pressing, [if] the delusive thoughts suddenly stop for a single thought, and suddenly body and mind drop away into emptiness, one then sees the great earth with not an inch of soil, deep beyond the infinite, and a great terror arises. If one does not break through this, one dares not go forward. Or one takes this expansive emptiness as something superb and wondrous. If one grasps this emptiness, then a great perverse view arises, denying cause and effect — this is the most dangerous point.]

Fifth, do not give rise to a mind of terror. When the power of thought in the work is urgent and pressing, and the delusive thoughts suddenly stop for a single thought, and suddenly body and mind drop away into emptiness, one then sees the great earth with not an inch of soil, deep beyond the infinite, and a great terror arises. If one does not break through such a state, one dares not go forward. Or one takes this expansive emptiness (everything empty) as a superb and wondrous state. If one grasps this emptiness as a superb and wondrous state, then a great perverse view arises, and one no longer believes in cause and effect — this is the most dangerous pass.
[Denying cause and effect (bowu yinguo)] Negating cause and effect. “Bo” means to cast away. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “Denying cause and effect, going entirely into emptiness.”

[SIXTH, be firmly resolved to believe that your own mind is Buddha. Yet there is no other Buddha besides this; the mind itself is it. Because the Buddha's true Dharma-body is like empty space. If one realizes that delusion is originally empty, then the originally present Dharma-body reveals itself of itself, bright and still, perfect and all-pervading, without lack and without excess. Do not again let the mind run outward in pursuit; if one abandons this mind and seeks elsewhere, then in the mind there arise all sorts of countless dream realms. These are precisely the manifestations of the consciousness-spirit; one must absolutely not regard them as anything extraordinary. Yet, in my pure and clear mind, there is originally no thing, and not even a single thought. Whenever one gives rise to a thought and sets the mind moving, that already violates the substance of the Dharma.]

Sixth, be firmly resolved to believe that your own mind is Buddha. Yet there is no other Buddha besides this; the mind itself is it. Because the Buddha's true Dharma-body is like empty space. If one realizes that delusions are originally false, then the originally present Dharma-body reveals itself of itself, bright and still, perfect and all-pervading, without lack and without excess. Do not again let the mind run outward in pursuit; if one abandons this mind and seeks elsewhere besides it, then in the mind there arise all sorts of countless dream realms. These are precisely the illusory manifestations of the consciousness-spirit; one must absolutely not regard them as anything extraordinary. You should know that in my pure and clear mind there is originally no thing, and not even a single thought. Whenever one gives rise to a thought and sets the mind moving, that already departs from the substance of the Dharma.

[SEVENTH, one must know that delusive thoughts are originally false. Those doing the work now generally do not know that the delusive thoughts of their own mind are originally false. They take these delusive thoughts to be real, and only make an adversary of them. This is like a child playing with the shadow of a lamp: the more one plays with it the less relations one has with it, and playing long enough one comes to be frightened by it. There is another kind, who fear delusive thoughts and wish they could seize them and cast them aside. This is like grasping at the wind and catching at shadows; all day long one wrestles with them, using up all one's strength, and never for a single thought is there respite. Entangled for so long, one's faith day by day grows weary. One then says that Chan practice has no efficacy, and gives rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of retreat — this is a common ailment of beginners. There is no other reason for it than that one has not understood that the abiding true mind is of a nature neither arising nor ceasing, and only takes delusive thoughts to be real Dharmas. Here one must absolutely pass through; if one would pass through this barrier, there is naturally an upward-road beyond.]

Seventh, one must know that delusive thoughts are originally false. Those doing the work now generally do not know that the delusive thoughts of their own mind are originally false. They take these delusive thoughts to be real, and only make an adversary of them. This is like a child playing with the shadow of a lamp: the more one plays with it the less relations one has with it, and playing long enough one becomes frightened by the shadow of the lamp itself. (This is to say: if one takes delusive thoughts to be real and makes an adversary of them, it is like a child playing with the shadow of himself on a wall — not only do the delusive thoughts fail to cease, but the more one plays the stranger it becomes, and after a long while it seems like a devil, and one is frightened.) There are another kind, who fear delusive thoughts and wish they could seize them and cast them aside. This is like grasping at the wind and catching at shadows; all day long one rolls about with them, using up all one's strength, and never for a single thought is there respite. Entangled for so long, one's faith day by day grows weary. One then says that Chan practice has no efficacy, and gives rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of retreat — this is a common ailment of those beginning to learn. There is no other reason for it than that one has not understood that the abiding true mind is of a nature neither arising nor ceasing, and only takes delusive thoughts to be real Dharmas. Here one must absolutely pass through; if one can pass this barrier, there is naturally an upward-road beyond.

[EIGHTH, one has only to investigate apart from mind and consciousness and seek apart from the realm of delusive thoughts. As soon as a thought arises, whether good or evil, set it aside on the spot; absolutely do not make an adversary of it. Truly believe that in your own mind there is originally no such thing. Just take up the huatou [you are] investigating and lift it with effort, like the vajra sword, striking down both demons and Buddhas. Here one most needs great courage, great vigor, and great endurance. One absolutely must not calculate front and back, and absolutely must not be timid and weak. Only with a straight mind and right thought, bracing oneself and going forward, will one naturally stand lofty and imposing, not entangled by these delusive thoughts, like a hawk that has slipped free of the leather armguard. Through all the hours of the day and night, amid all circumstances and conditions, one is naturally not obstructed and fettered, naturally attaining great ease and great freedom — this is the point where the beginner gains strength in the first step of the work.]

Eighth, one has only to investigate apart from mind and consciousness and seek apart from the realm of delusive thoughts. As soon as a thought arises, whether it be good or evil, set it aside on the spot; absolutely do not make an adversary of it. Truly believe that in your own mind there is originally no such thing. Just take up the huatou [you are] investigating and lift it with effort, like the vajra sword — when a demon (an evil thought) comes, cut down the demon; when a Buddha (a good thought) comes, cut down the Buddha. Here one most needs great courage, great vigor, and great endurance. One absolutely must not calculate front and back, and absolutely must not be timid and hesitant. Only with a straight mind and right thought, bracing oneself and going forward, will one naturally stand lofty and imposing, not entangled by these delusive thoughts, like a hawk that has slipped free of the leather armguard, freely soaring. Through all the hours of the day and night, amid all circumstances and conditions, one is naturally not obstructed and fettered, naturally attaining great ease and great freedom — this is the point where the beginner gains strength in the first step of the work.

[Mind (xin), intention (yi), and consciousness (shi)] Mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna), intention refers to the seventh consciousness (the manas), and consciousness refers to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness). [A hawk that has slipped free of the armguard (tuo gou zhi ying)] Like a hawk whose leg strap is released and that escapes the leather armguard — a metaphor for no longer being constrained; gou
gōu
was a leather armguard worn when shooting arrows in ancient times.

[The several points above are much like drawing legs on a snake — they are but provisional words for the occasion. They are not the ultimate, nor are they real Dharmas. It is because, being on the road, fearing that at the first step out the door one may fall into the divergent bypaths, wasting effort of mind and vainly losing time, [I have spoken them]. One must truly take the one gate that exits onto the sublime and wonderful path of adornment. What is called walking evenly and uprightly, swift as the wind: in one's course one can multiply a day into a kalpa. In short, the upward-road of the Buddhas and patriarchs does not involve a journey's length; yet for the beginner's expedient means, one must also pass through from here.]

The several points I have spoken above are much like drawing legs on a snake — they are but provisional words for the occasion. They are not the ultimate, nor are they real Dharmas. Because you have already set out on the road, fearing only that you might err at this first step out the door, stray into a wrong path, waste effort of mind, and vainly lose time, I have reluctantly spoken these words. In cultivation one must take a true path to Buddhahood (the sublime and wonderful path of adornment that exits through the one gate). If the path is right and the method also right (walking evenly and uprightly, swift as the wind), then the swiftness of advance is like what would require a whole kalpa to attain, now attained in a single day. In short, the upward-road of the Buddhas and patriarchs does not require going so great a distance or spending so long a time to realize the fruit. Even at the first step of a beginner, one must understand this principle.

[The one gate that exits onto the sublime and wonderful path of adornment (yimen chaochu miao zhuangyan lu)] The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “At that time the World-Honored One, in the midst of the assembly, stretched out his golden arm and stroked Ānanda's head, and instructed Ānanda and the great assembly: There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha's Crown Heroic Śūraṅgama King, endowed with all practices; by this one gate the Tathāgatas of the ten directions exit onto the sublime and wonderful path of adornment.” The full title of the Śūraṅgama Sutra is “The Sutra of the Great Buddha's Crown, the Tathāgata's secret cause, the ultimate meaning of cultivation and realization, the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas, the Heroic Śūraṅgama.” [The Heroic Śūraṅgama (shou lengyan)] The name of the samādhi attained by the Buddha. [Course (xinglü)] Walking. [The upward-road of the Buddhas and patriarchs does not involve a journey's length] The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Yet there is quickness and slowness in realizing this mind. There are those who, upon hearing the Dharma, in a single thought attain the mind of no-mind; there are those who attain the mind of no-mind only upon reaching the ten stages of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; there are those who attain the mind of no-mind only upon reaching the ten grounds. Whether long or short, only when one attains the mind of no-mind is one settled; there is then nothing more to be cultivated or realized. In truth there is nothing attained — this is genuinely not false. One who attains in a single thought and one who attains on the tenth ground have exactly the same function, with no greater or lesser depth; it is merely that through many eons one has vainly undergone toil.”
